arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (`el registro de decisiones la política de trazado`). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. Los bytes de la imagen no se guardan nunca —no hay clave que los active— y el `pedido` solo si `[retencion] pedido = true`. Lo que se vacía son **campos**, y que estaban vaciados queda registrado (la regla de qué se versiona): la corrida conserva su `corrida_id`, su ordinal, sus rankings y sus degradaciones, porque borrarla reasignaría el ordinal y un informe que cita la corrida #1 apuntaría a otra ejecución.

aic:16405.texto:
In this allegorical painting, a personification of Innocence at center signals her preference for Love, represented as a cupid, over Riches, taking the form of a woman in lavish Grecian robes and offering a chest of golden baubles. Pierre-Paul Prud’hon complicated this straightforward parable by manipulating the figures’ postures: while Innocence embraces Love, she gazes longingly over her shoulder at Riches, inviting viewers to wonder about the finality of her decision.
Prud’hon created this preparatory sketch for a larger painting to be completed by his collaborator and friend, Constance Mayer, who was known for her portraits and allegorical scenes.
aic:16405.title: Innocence Prefers Love to Riches

aic:16488.texto:
This painting likely once graced a large hall at the Palazzo Corner in Venice along with several others. The suite illustrates the ill-fated love of Armida and Rinaldo from Torquato Tasso’s 1581 epic poem Gerusalemme liberata (Jerusalem Delivered). The story takes place during the First Crusade, an eleventh-century military expedition in which Christian knights attempted to seize control of Jerusalem and check the power of the Muslims who ruled the city. In this scene, the beautiful sorceress Armida encounters the knight Rinaldo as he sleeps and decides to carry him away on her cloud-borne chariot. When Rinaldo wakes, he immediately falls for Armida and forgets his quest in Jerusalem.
Giovanni Battista Tiepolo painted a vast, open expanse of sky and scenery and elaborately arranged the figures, draperies, clouds, and trees to animate the composition. Although Tasso’s story symbolizes the conflict between love and duty, Tiepolo’s depiction of a magical world—enhanced by effervescent colors and dense, creamy paint—seems to evoke only love’s enchantment.
Tiepolo’s paintings combine virtuosic draftsmanship with seemingly spontaneous execution, a formula perfectly suited to the large-scale works that he created to decorate palaces and churches throughout Italy, Germany, and Spain.
aic:16488.title: Armida Encounters the Sleeping Rinaldo

aic:16488.texto: Possibly one of four scenes from Tasso made for the 'gabinetto degli specchi' of the Palazzo Corner a San Polo, Venice [according to inventories and other documents discussed by Romanelli 1998]. Count Giovanni Serbelloni, Venice in 1838; by descent, until possibly 1886 [Molmenti 1911 and Knox 1978]. Giulio Cartier, Genoa by 1908 [Malaquzzi Valeri 1908]; Sedelmeyer Gallery, Paris, in 1912 [Ojetti 1912]; James Deering (d. 1925), Vizcaya, from 1913 [information sheet in curatorial file]; bequeathed,1925.
aic:16488.title: Armida Encounters the Sleeping Rinaldo

aic:36492.texto: This painting presents an allegory of the virtue of charity through images of maternal love and sacrifice: a mother nurtures several young children and a pelican feeds her young by drawing blood from her own breast. This work was one of a set of allegories of five virtues intended as decorations set above doors in a palace belonging to the king of Savoy, a region in northwest Italy. Francesco de Mura spent most of his career in Naples but also worked for the king of Savoy in the 1740s, producing paintings in a style that combined grand, calm figures with active drapery. Although it is now rectangular, the canvas shows signs of an earlier curved shape appropriate to a Rococo room decoration.
aic:36492.title: Allegory of Charity

aic:36492.texto: Probably commissioned by Charles Emmanuel III, Turin [see Pinto 1987]. Peretti, Rome, by 1971 [according to Heim Commission Book at the Getty Research Institute]; Heim Gallery, London, 1971; sold to the Art Institute, 1971.
aic:36492.title: Allegory of Charity

cma:134620.texto:
Is this painting by Titian?

Titian, the celebrated and prolific 16th-century Venetian artist, and his large workshop painted several versions of this subject. Further research is needed to compare this painting with versions in Milan and Madrid to determine how much of each is by Titian himself, as opposed to being the work of his studio assistants. The Prado Museum in Madrid is often considered to have a copy made from Cleveland’s painting, which is superior in execution but not condition. Despite the damage caused by overcleaning, there are many fine passages, including the bowing white horse, his groom in shadow, and the cradled Christ child.
cma:134620.title: Adoration of the Magi

cma:134620.texto: This painting is filled with naturalistic details such as the riders who struggle to keep their horses and mules still and a small dog who urinates on a beam.

cma:150077.texto: The subject of this painting comes from the 16th-century Spanish novel Lazarillo de Tormes. This tells the story of Lazarillo, a poor servant boy who worked for an impoverished blind man. Abused by his master, and never given enough to eat or drink, Lazarillo is forced to fend for himself. According to the story, he steals wine by drinking it from a straw directly from the blind man's jug. This painting relates to a cultural movement known as espagnolisme, the French interest in Spanish art and literature. Especially popular during the 1850s, espagnolisme focused upon realistic, often down-trodden characters such as Lazarillo. Instead of finding them naïve or foolishly humorous, artists such as Ribot related to their alienation from society and found inspiration in the detailed descriptions of their rough, lowly lifestyles.
cma:150077.title: Lazarillo de Tormes and His Blind Master

afirmaciones.texto: La obra presenta una alegoría de la virtud de la caridad a través de imágenes de amor maternal y sacrificio, mostrando a una madre que alimenta a varios niños y a un pelícano que alimenta a sus crías con su propia sangre.
La representación de la caridad como amor y sacrificio maternal sugiere una interpretación de generosidad profunda y desinteresada.
La pintura es una alegoría en la que la Inocencia prefiere el Amor a las Riquezas, mostrando un conflicto entre valores materiales y afectivos.
La obra sugiere una tensión en la elección de la Inocencia, lo que puede interpretarse como una generosidad emocional pero con dudas o ambivalencias.
La pintura representa a Lazarillo, un niño pobre y sirviente que sufre abuso y privaciones, y debe valerse por sí mismo.
La obra se centra en personajes marginados y sus difíciles condiciones, lo que no se asocia directamente con la generosidad sino con la lucha y la supervivencia.
La pintura ilustra la historia de Armida y Rinaldo, donde Armida decide llevarse al caballero dormido, evocando el poder del amor y el abandono del deber.
La escena se enfoca en el encanto y la magia del amor, pero no en la generosidad como virtud explícita.
La obra representa la Adoración de los Magos, un tema que implica la entrega de regalos al niño Jesús, acto que puede interpretarse como generosidad.
El tema de la adoración con regalos sugiere un acto de generosidad, aunque el fragmento no detalla explícitamente la generosidad como virtud central.

Por eso la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica y lo que rige es **escritura única** (la escritura única del plan). lo que no entra en la identidad del plan: `α`, N, la fusión y el `variante_id` **no** son ingredientes. la versión del prompt como ingrediente del plan: el prompt **+ su versión**, el modelo y el muestreo **sí**.
plan.nota_de_pl3: Las **tres** cláusulas van escritas porque son **tres cosas**: que las dos consultas existan, que difieran del pedido crudo (*rewriting*) y que difieran entre sí (lo que distingue *expansion* de *rewriting*). El veredicto viaja adentro para que las tres cláusulas de las consultas del plan se pueda contar **también sobre una ad-hoc**, cuyo pedido el registro de decisiones no deja guardar.
plan.nota_de_pl5: la escritura única del plan: un `plan_id` se escribe **una sola vez**; si ya existe se **lee** y la corrida registra si lo **produjo o lo reusó**. Sin ese registro no habría forma de saber **qué corrida pagó la llamada que la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura cuenta**.

formato.nota: El formato concreto **sigue abierto**: esto es la **cosmética declarada**, no el contrato. El contrato —`[n]` que asigna el renderizador, toda afirmación con dato citando un `fragment_id` recuperado en esta consulta, 100 % de los CC-BY con atribución, español + cita textual en inglés— vive en el código y es el conteo de referencias colgadas, el criterio de atribución, el criterio de idioma y las obligaciones de la cita.

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**. La cita viaja desde `knowledge` hasta acá **sin pasar por el modelo** (el contrato de salida), y las obligaciones de la cita lo verifica byte a byte: si el formateo viviera dentro del prompt, *'textual'* dependería de que el modelo no lo reescriba.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “The subject of this painting comes from the 16th-century Spanish novel Lazarillo de Tormes. This tells the story of Lazarillo, a poor servant boy who worked for an impoverished blind man. Abused by his master, and never given enough to eat or drink, Lazarillo is forced to fend for himself. According to the story, he steals wine by drinking it from a straw directly from the blind man's jug. This painting relates to a cultural movement known as espagnolisme, the French interest in Spanish art and literature. Especially popular during the 1850s, espagnolisme focused upon realistic, often down-trodden characters such as Lazarillo. Instead of finding them naïve or foolishly humorous, artists such as Ribot related to their alienation from society and found inspiration in the detailed descriptions of their rough, lowly lifestyles.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1980.282 · CC0 1.0

4. **Armida Encounters the Sleeping Rinaldo**
   Giovanni Battista Tiepolo · c. 1742–45 · Oil on canvas · Baroque
   Ficha oficial: https://www.artic.edu/artworks/16488

   La pintura ilustra la historia de Armida y Rinaldo, donde Armida decide llevarse al caballero dormido, evocando el poder del amor y el abandono del deber. [1]
   La escena se enfoca en el encanto y la magia del amor, pero no en la generosidad como virtud explícita.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “This painting likely once graced a large hall at the Palazzo Corner in Venice along with several others. The suite illustrates the ill-fated love of Armida and Rinaldo from Torquato Tasso’s 1581 epic poem Gerusalemme liberata (Jerusalem Delivered). The story takes place during the First Crusade, an eleventh-century military expedition in which Christian knights attempted to seize control of Jerusalem and check the power of the Muslims who ruled the city. In this scene, the beautiful sorceress Armida encounters the knight Rinaldo as he sleeps and decides to carry him away on her cloud-borne chariot. When Rinaldo wakes, he immediately falls for Armida and forgets his quest in Jerusalem.
Giovanni Battista Tiepolo painted a vast, open expanse of sky and scenery and elaborately arranged the figures, draperies, clouds, and trees to animate the composition. Although Tasso’s story symbolizes the conflict between love and duty, Tiepolo’s depiction of a magical world—enhanced by effervescent colors and dense, creamy paint—seems to evoke only love’s enchantment.
Tiepolo’s paintings combine virtuosic draftsmanship with seemingly spontaneous execution, a formula perfectly suited to the large-scale works that he created to decorate palaces and churches throughout Italy, Germany, and Spain.”
       https://www.artic.edu/artworks/16488 · CC BY 4.0
       “Armida Encounters the Sleeping Rinaldo”, Giovanni Battista Tiepolo. Art Institute of Chicago. Texto bajo CC BY 4.0 — https://www.artic.edu/artworks/16488

5. **Adoration of the Magi**
   Titian · 1500s · oil on canvas
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1957.150

   La obra representa la Adoración de los Magos, un tema que implica la entrega de regalos al niño Jesús, acto que puede interpretarse como generosidad. [1]
   El tema de la adoración con regalos sugiere un acto de generosidad, aunque el fragmento no detalla explícitamente la generosidad como virtud central.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “Is this painting by Titian?

Titian, the celebrated and prolific 16th-century Venetian artist, and his large workshop painted several versions of this subject. Further research is needed to compare this painting with versions in Milan and Madrid to determine how much of each is by Titian himself, as opposed to being the work of his studio assistants. The Prado Museum in Madrid is often considered to have a copy made from Cleveland’s painting, which is superior in execution but not condition. Despite the damage caused by overcleaning, there are many fine passages, including the bowing white horse, his groom in shadow, and the cradled Christ child.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1957.150 · CC0 1.0
